utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There are a few procedural matters I understood the parties wanted to raise. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If -- I only raise the question of where we are as far as witnesses are concerned. Mr. Josse is going to deal with one or two other matters, if he may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As far as witnesses are concerned, I have informed the Trial Chamber, but this brings Mr. Krajisnik immediately up-to-date as well, Your Honour, if I may, because I haven't had a chance to discuss it with him. Happily, Mr. Lakic is able to travel tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we were informed about that, that the withdrawal of his visa was cancelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, as you were, so that's good with Mr. Lakic. The other piece of encouraging news, Your Honour, is that Mr. Maricic, the next witness, is able to travel on Saturday. All the technicalities have been taken care of, it's been confirmed that he will travel. Your Honour, if I may just look ahead to indicate a problem that may arise but might not, and just to flag it. Mr. Maricic arriving on Saturday, the Court is sitting on Monday morning next week. Your Honour, depending on what happens with other witnesses, Your Honours can see straight away that the only opportunity -- or the first opportunity we would have to go and see Mr. Krajisnik with Mr. Maricic would be Monday morning. It is quite impossible to go over the weekend, Your Honour. Just in case there was any chance, I've checked that and have been told unequivocally that's not possible. But, Your Honour, whether that in fact creates a difficulty will depend on the progress we make with this next witness, Mr. Radojko, and then the progress we make with Mr. Lakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I mention one other thing, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time already, explore the possibility of not sitting in the morning of Tuesday, the 22nd [sic] of March. But as you know, Friday afternoon and Monday morning are not the most attractive --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I recognise that, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we already inquire into possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, may I just mention this as well, looking ahead, that perhaps we might bear in mind that Mr. Lakic, though as far as we know in good health, is quite an elderly man, Your Honour, and he's perhaps not -- not able to undertake the same sort of programme that sometimes we do undertake with witnesses; fairly heavy meetings and schedules when they arrive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think information received -- this information already came to the Chamber when earlier he was expected to arrive. So that's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm obliged, Your Honour, I'm never quite sure exactly what information has reached everybody in all this, but there it is. And Mr. Maricic is of a similar age, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that, Mr. Stewart. Then there is a motion pending pursuant to Rule 90 bis. It has been filed on the 10th of March. It's an urgent motion. I do not know whether the time up until the 23rd of March, and then, I take it, preferably one or two days before that date, will be enough. I see on your schedule that the Defence would like to have the witness, at latest, at Tuesday, the 21st of March. The only thing I can say is that to file a motion 11 days in advance is not a guarantee for success. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the position of the Prosecutor's Office that we will not file a written reply to this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we deal with the matter in open court?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before I give you an opportunity to respond, Mr. Harmon - and I apologise for interrupting you - Mr. Stewart, I hope you'll forgive me that I do not know all the criminal codes by heart. 211 and 226 of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska deal with what type of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have -- I have no more idea than Your Honour, but Mr. Josse may have slightly more idea than both of us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I take it that at least what the Defence would have done in respect of a Defence witness, to see whether there is any overlap with the questions to be put to the witness in the present case, because if the witness would come and would tell us only that by answering questions he would incriminate himself -- I've got no idea what this is. Is this economic crimes, are these war crimes, are these crimes against -- crimes against humanity? I've got no idea, and I think it's relevant for the Defence to know in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, two things: First of all, I'm quite confident Mr. Josse can tell you more than I can straight away, Your Honour, but also we have in mind that, even if there is an overlap, the Court, in the usual way, as it has done previously in this case, can direct a witness to answer on the basis that his answers are not to be used against him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You will understand - and I think that's a matter that has been raised before - that of course we could check with the Prosecution in this court, and perhaps the Prosecution is aware of what type of charges were brought against -- against the witness, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Josse knows. Should I just hand straight on to him, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Because we're proceeding on the basis of something neither Your Honour nor I know about and we have someone in court who does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: First of all may I say, Your Honour, we did not find it very easy obtaining this information. The source is not as reliable as, frankly, I might have hoped. That is one of the reasons we delayed submitting the motion. But eventually the time arrived where we took the decision that we could wait no longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. When you say "the information was not easy to obtain," are you talking about the content of the articles of the criminal code?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not the contents of the code, as such, but exactly - and I mean exactly - what this gentleman is doing in prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I can tell you that it has nothing to do with alleged war crimes; it's to do with an alleged fraud that occurred after the war had ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, the matter has been reported on the Tribunet briefly, and has been widely reported in the media in the Republika Srpska. So I'm fairly confident about that. Your Honour, for what it's worth, his co-accused, who's also in custody in the Republika Srpska, is Momcilo Mandic. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, now at least the Chamber can understand that on the basis of the charges brought against this witness at this moment in Republika Srpska that we do not have to fear that more than you could, in general terms, expect with witnesses, that he would -- he would refrain from answering questions for -- out of fear of self-incrimination, apart from the general fear, perhaps, that exists, but that usually is dealt with this OTP, whereas of course what happens in Republika Srpska is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I say Your Honour is very wise with respect to use the word "general" because I suspect this witness might have general concerns, from what I understand. But these matters have got nothing to do with those general concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand that he was in a prison in the Sarajevo area. He's been moved out of that prison for logistical reasons, so I am told. He has made a relatively recent contact with connections of ours in the Republika Srpska from his prison cell, as I understand it - this is at least second-hand hearsay, let me make it absolutely plain, not least because of the language difficulties - has again expressed his willingness to come to this court and give evidence, subject to physically being able to and being brought here, and I hope that assists a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There's a little bit more information I may have if Your Honour has any specific questions, but I can't promise to be terribly helpful, and could I emphasise that really the information I'm relaying to the Court, of course I'm doing it genuinely, but it's based on pretty limited sources of information despite the best efforts of one member of our team in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood and accepted. Mr. Harmon, response to the motion orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will not file a written response to the motion. I direct the Court's attention to paragraph 4, relief sought; paragraph 8 subpart (ii), we fully subscribe to that portion and we would request that when he arrives here that he not be in contact in the prison with the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The request 8(ii) says more, and says: "Protected from inference by other persons." That would be a bit broader. I mean, would it be sufficient for you if he would be not in contact with the accused in the Detention Unit, or would you like to have him separated from others in that Detention Unit as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, our preference is to have him separated from others in the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we couldn't object to this gentleman being separated from our client or, indeed, anyone else in the prison, but I am sure that in the normal course of events we would ask that he see Mr. Krajisnik in the presence of one of us, as per any other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's then clear. The Chamber will then deal with the matter at a -- as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for having to confer for a second. Yes, the Chamber will give a decision as soon as possible. Then I think we still -- we have a few other matters. First of all, I think, Mr. Josse, that you would still need five minutes to respond to the Prosecution's submissions in relation to the Savkic exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, yes, I hope I'll be very much less than that. I'm very grateful to Your Honour's opportunity to return to this subject because we have considered the matter further. I have discussed it, in particular, with Mr. Stewart, who wasn't in court when the matter was last debated, so to speak. So far as P1055 is concerned, we have changed our stance. Having considered very carefully Your Honour's observations, so far as my submissions are concerned, we are now of the view that that document should be admitted into evidence. We accept that it would be, frankly, nonsensical to not admit it into evidence, bearing in mind it purports to come from the witness. And we accept that the issue as to whether or not it's a forgery has nothing to do with its admission into evidence. I repeat, in a sentence, of course the Court is going to need to decide whether it is a forgery. I've made my submissions as to where the burden of proof relies in relation to that, where the standard of proof lies in relation to that, and my submissions have not changed at all as far as that is concerned. But notwithstanding that, whether the Court finds it is a forgery, it isn't a forgery, isn't sure it's a forgery, we do accept it should be admitted into evidence so that the matter can be considered properly by the Chamber. Your Honour, in a further sentence, we do invite the Court to treat that completely differently to our main grounds for objection in relation to documents which contain second- or third-hand hearsay which are put to the witness and which the witness then completely refutes, because in effect that's trying to get 92 bis-type evidence in through the book door. This document, 1055, doesn't fall into that category, and we withdraw our objection to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. Josse, this Chamber has accepted, to some extent, what we called contextual exhibits. And if a witness doesn't recognise the document, that would not automatically exclude that exhibit from being relevant and being admissible as a contextual exhibit, but perhaps we should clearly separate that and see that if a witness says "I don't know that document," that it could not be admitted through that witness, which does not, under all circumstances, would exclude the exhibit to be admitted as a contextual exhibit. That's -- this is just a thought, this is not a decision, but a --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, you can see, Mr. Stewart is anxious to try and discuss the matter with me further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take your time, it's not urgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We're grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think these were -- Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There was one additional matter, Your Honour, and that is the request by the Prosecution to have relief from the deadline --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- for an item that is found in the Court's 2nd of March, 2006, omnibus order on the admission of exhibits and related requests. I refer specifically to page 3 of that decision dealing with contracts and other material relating to Prosecution Exhibit 340. And in that, this was an exhibit, Your Honour, that dealt with the relinquishment of property on allegedly a voluntary basis in order to leave municipalities. The Court had ordered the Prosecution to provide the requested documents to the Chamber and the Defence within two weeks of this order. As I mentioned earlier, I had a limited number of such documents. I had been in contact through my investigator with an agency in Bosnia that said that they had a large number of these documents. My investigator went to that agency, was informed that the agency had neither the time nor resources to comply with the Court's order, and we couldn't get them in time. They suggested, instead, that we go to the various municipalities in the ARK where such repositories of such documents existed. Now, I have at this point in time directed my investigator to do just that, subject to a Court's decision giving me some relief from the deadline of this for compliance, which is the 16th of March. What I propose, Your Honour, is the Court put -- grant my request for additional relief, additional time. I will then send my investigator to 11 municipalities within the ARK, those 11 being the municipalities that have been touched upon in the evidence before the Court, as opposed to 21 municipalities, some of which have never been touched upon, and my investigator will then collect representative samples as the Court has requested. He cannot do that by the 16th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time does he need?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I need to be in touch with him. I would say two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two weeks more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Two weeks more from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, any objection to granting an additional two weeks?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your request is granted, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got two other matters. One I alluded to on Friday, that is the issue to do with D14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour originally gave us to today and then very kindly granted an extension. The position is this: I have a person -- bearing in mind it was me he was effectively referring to in the course of his evidence -- we'll assume it was me when he talked about Defence counsel because I was the Defence counsel who dealt with it. I have a limited recollection of this. The member of our team who is responsible for these matters is away for another week. I would request two weeks. In that time, I will speak, of course, to the member of the team when he returns, instruct him to try and find the document, and if he doesn't, then to try and contact D14. We would like to be as cooperative as we can about the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, you were given 14 days, now you are asked 14 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, we do not object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Granted, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next matter, Your Honour, are the exhibits related to Mr. Poplasen. I am not yet in a position to tell the Court which I wish to argue and which I don't, but it may be, for Mr. Harmon's benefit, the Court would like to fix a date for him to return here, bearing in mind I think he is not dealing with the next witness, for that argument to take place. The vast majority I am not going to argue, I can already tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you inform Mr. Harmon when you are ready and inform the Chamber at the same time, then we will find a suitable moment to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's wait until that moment for all exhibits introduced through Mr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the last matter relates to the next witness and it's not really a procedural matter, it relates to his testimony, so I'll turn to that when the Court is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There -- the last witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did I say the last witness? Yes, I beg your pardon, the next witness. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Next witness, I beg your pardon. It relates to Mr. Radojko. It's introduction, so to speak, a preliminary observation-cum-submission that I wish to make before he commences his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I take it that you want to make that observation in his absence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there's no other procedural matter to be raised, so therefore, Mr. Harmon and Mr. Margetts, I see that you're about to leave, so you're excused. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the flurry of e-mails this morning between the Chamber, Mr. Tieger, and Mr. Stewart, I was aware of a potential difficulty so far as the transcript of this witness's evidence in the Brdjanin trial. I personally didn't deal with the matter this morning because I was in the UNDU, seeing Mr. Krajisnik. The difficulty that I was aware of was this: Mr. Radojko was originally due to give live evidence at this court in April of 2004. There is no dispute that he came to The Hague, he waited for about five days, he didn't get on, and he was sent home. Thereafter, as I understand it, the Prosecution sought to have his evidence in Brdjanin, which lasted about four days, admitted pursuant to 92 bis. I assume that two members of this Chamber read those transcripts and one did not, simply because of the time-span involved because Judge Hanoteau wasn't a member of the Bench at that particular juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see in -- you would -- why do you think that the two other Judges would have read those transcripts?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, I was under the impression that if a piece of evidence is going to be admitted 92 bis, then the Judges would have had to have read it in order, one, to decide if it can be admitted, and, two, then to decide if it should be admitted subject to cross-examination. So that's why I make that assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was confused when you said the person who you sought to have his evidence in Brdjanin admitted pursuant to 92 bis. That's fine, but none of these Judges have -- we are not -- now I do understand, yes, and I misread you, admission not in Brdjanin under 92 bis, but the transcript of his Brdjanin testimony to be admitted under Rule 92 bis in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Precisely. So I'm assuming that that's, albeit a long time ago - almost two years ago - these four days of evidence was read by two of the present members of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least there's a fair chance that if we have not seen every letter of it, then at least we have seen quite some of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thereafter, the Court, as I've already said, ordered that Mr. Radojko attend for cross-examination; and thereafter that, the Prosecution decided to drop him as a witness, I accept, on grounds of time and expediency. If I'm wrong about that, Mr. Tieger will correct me, but he and I have discussed the matter briefly this morning and I'm sure that is correct. So the Prosecution, having to make ruthless decisions about time, decided not to call Mr. Radojko in those circumstances. So my first observation prior to Mr. Tieger's e-mail of this morning was there's a certain imbalance, because two members of the Court have read, at least if not in whole, part of the evidence and the other has not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the last assumption is not a correct one. Judge Hanoteau has familiarised himself with the case and that does not say that he has only read transcripts and -- so therefore -- I mean, I hope that you were not under the impression that whatever happened before the arrival of Judge Hanoteau was unknown to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For weeks and weeks he worked hard to get acquainted, but of course I would not know whether -- I would not even know for myself how -- if I read it all, but I have the habit of reading things very intensive, but I could not say, of course, the same for Judge Hanoteau, and I think it's not a matter to -- it's not a question to be answered in detail at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But your assumption that two of the Judges would be familiar with the material and the third would not be is an assumption that I cannot at this moment accept as a correct assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Moving on from that, and frankly I don't think it matters a great deal, the Defence position is that we're not relying on the transcripts in Brdjanin and we don't wish to have those admitted under 92 bis. And I simply want to be clear that that is the present procedure. I, of course, accept that Mr. Tieger is able to cross-examine the witness with any proper material that he can use, and that obviously includes the transcripts from a previous trial. That's obviously material that can be used in the course of cross-examination, but I simply want and need to be clear that this transcript, four-day transcript, is not part of the evidence as we stand at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I never understood anything to the contrary, Your Honour, and I am not aware of any communication between the parties or to the Court that would have suggested otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I don't remember exactly what happened two years ago. I take it that you have submitted for admission 92 bis material from Mr. Radojko, that we may have decided that you would have -- that that material was admitted into evidence but that Mr. Radojko should be called for cross-examination. Is that -- that you then said: We're not going to call Mr. Radojko. And I'm not certain anymore whether we then took a decision that you withdraw that 92 bis material because you couldn't meet the condition set by the Chamber or whether the Chamber decided that it was not any longer in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Irrespective of the precise procedural background, Your Honour, it is not the Prosecution's impression or position that those transcripts are in evidence or that the Defence has sought to tender them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I -- and as I say, I don't know if there was a misimpression to that effect, but I hope that clarifies it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll -- of course we'll check -- for the Chamber it's important to know exactly what the procedural steps have been that were taken, and my memory just doesn't serve me at this moment, which at least means, Mr. Josse, that this Chamber has not prepared itself by studying these -- these transcripts. So therefore, we'll check it during the first break, but we start the examination of Mr. Radojko on the basis that nothing of any written statement -- of any written statement is in evidence at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just add this because, since I was here at that time - I have been always here, Your Honour; Mr. Josse wasn't - it was always the assumption on the Defence side that where material had been admitted under 92 bis subject to the witness being produced for cross-examination, that if the witness then were not produced for cross-examination, that 92 bis -- that would automatically lapse, that it simply would fall out of evidence without any further technical step being taken, but the practical result may be the same, however, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to know whether we took any practical steps or whether it's on the basis of what you just said that this material is not in evidence. Mr. Josse, are you ready to call Mr. Radojko?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, could you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radojko. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I do hear you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radojko. Please be seated. For those who listened on the English channel, I heard "... that I shall speak ..." It reads "... I will speak ..." I take it that in the original language it's "will" and not "shall," which, of course, is a different -- I take it that you solemnly declare that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, Mr. Radojko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There was a translation issue. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What's your name, please?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: My name is Jovo Radojko.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were born in the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's right you, in fact, went to higher --

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... school in Zagreb in about 1981?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You then went to the political science faculty in Zagreb, intending to become a journalist. You didn't complete that and went, instead, to law school?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. Afterwards I decided to switch over to the law school.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You received your diploma from Zagreb University law school in 1987 and worked in Zagreb in 1990, until you passed the bar exam?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You worked for a time in Croatia, but due to ethnic difficulties, you took a job that you were offered in Petrovac in the same year?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the end of 1990 you were appointed secretary of the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as your political involvement is concerned, you were a member of the Croatian SDS party, which you had joined in 1990?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then you remained a member of the SDS when you moved to Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The job of secretary of the Executive Committee you remained in until September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You then went with your family to Derventa and you were a judge there for approximately 10 years?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Nine years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact, in 2004 you were not re-appointed a judge in Petrovac due to issues involving ethnic quotas, and you've done various things since then and you're presently trying to qualify as a notary. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: During the war, as we've heard, you were secretary of the Executive Committee. You were also -- you also saw active service in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: On a number of occasions, I had been mobilised into the armed forces. I wasn't an active officer; I'm a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's right that, as you've said, on occasions you were mobilised to a unit and then you would return and continue your job as secretary to the Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want at this point to this deal with this matter in real outline, but it is right, isn't it, that after the Second World War there was a great deal of ill feeling by Serbs towards Muslims and Croats as a result of what had gone on during that war?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In communist times, were those feelings curtailed or contained in any real and serious way?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Well, there was constant mistrust amongst the population and a lack of sufferance, but the communist system and the communist regime was relentless in trying to discourage it. They were aware of the risk of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It may be important for some of your subsequent answers: Though you've just gone your history, you were away from Petrovac for a long period of time. We know you came back in 1990. When in fact did you leave the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I had never actually lived in Petrovac until 1990. My family had land on the territory of the municipality of Kljuc and only a part of what we had, some land and a flat, were in the municipality of Petrovac. I went to school in Kljuc, and I left there to go to Zagreb in 1974, and after 16 years, due to the circumstances, I arrived in Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, just to clarify a matter. One of your previous questions was about ill feelings, and the witness in his answer referred to mistrust, and then at the end of his answer he says: "They were aware of the risk of all that." I take it that the witness meant to say that the risk of the events experienced during the Second World War would repeat itself. Is that how I have to understand the risk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I suppose you have understood me well. What I meant to say was the communist leadership was aware of the risk involved in even discussing these issues, and they wanted to suppress them in every way possible, and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Assembly was a gentleman called Mr. Novakovic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Up until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When he was killed in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I know this is a generalisation, but as far as you could see, what sort of president was he? Did he do the job well?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Well, under the circumstances, he did it to the best of his ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And was he a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: He was. He was one of the leading SDS members within the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you immediately about the growth of criminal gangs in the municipality. When did it become apparent that there were criminal gangs operating in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact date, nor was this a phenomenon which came about all of a sudden. It is something that developed and started escalating gradually. Basically, as the war was spreading on the area of the former Yugoslavia, a certain number of people joined military units. Certain people because they were conscripted or mobilised, and others were volunteers. Amongst volunteers there were people who did not have an acceptable goal, so to say. There were people who went, donned uniforms, picked up arms, and when time came for them to take leave, because everybody would get leave in between periods of time spent on the front lines, they would go home but they would keep their weapons and their ammunition, and at least those people who had less-than noble intentions used a pretty simple method. The next time around, they wouldn't join the unit that they came from but another unit, and then they would take weapons there as well, and they kept quiet about their previous unit. Since the system was in a total disarray, they were able to do so; otherwise, under normal circumstances, they wouldn't have been able to get away with it. So in the end they didn't even go to war, as such, but those were people who were criminals or who had criminal intentions or tendencies, even before the war. So they declared themselves to be some kind of protection force of the people or whatever, but gradually they starting using this apparent participation and membership of the armed forces as an excuse in the public eye in order to avoid any pressure being brought to bear in the sense that they should be arrested, and they started using those weapons for less-than noble goals. For example, if they were arrested by the civilian police and they asked them for their IDs, they would be able to prove that they were members of the military, so they couldn't do anything about them. So they would turn to the military police, but in most cases they were too far away - in this particular case, in Croatia - and when the feedback came back, it would again be time for them to join the unit and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. That's quite a lot of information there. It's quite important perhaps to and define some sort of period. Help us, if you can, with when you say these gangs started to emerge in your municipality. If you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: In our area, at some point in the first half of 1992 was the first time that this was noticed as far as I can remember, and this was the first time that there was intervention on the part of the then-member of the National Assembly. He first initiated this and he asked for them to be stopped. I don't know whether at the time it was the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency, because they tended to change their name quite frequently, but I seem to remember that they asked the police administration to arrest those people because -- I mean, they couldn't actually order the police to do so, they could only ask them to do so. And that was the system back then. And I know there were some serious attempts as banning them from the area, even though they were not brought to trial. I know they were arrested. Some of them had been released, by force, by their own colleagues, so to say, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I have used the word "criminal gang" deliberately. By "criminal gang" -- let me start that again. In your mind, does "criminal gang" equate with paramilitary or are they different concepts and entities?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I'm going to give you my own personal opinion. I do know exactly what the distinction is and what the classification is, rather. I really do believe that there were criminal gangs, criminal groups, whatever you want to call them. There were several such groups appearing in our area. Some were chased away straight away; others dwelt a bit longer. The biggest problem was represented by those who originally came from the area because you couldn't chase them anywhere. Why do I think that they're not paramilitary units? In our area, there were no paramilitary units or formations because all those who were soldiers had their specific and well-determined affiliation. Paramilitary formations do have some kind of system of command and all that. I mean, this group normally exists in the shape and form of a military unit, even though it may not be within the framework of the official armed forces. But that's not who they were. They would don their uniforms, pick up their weapons, strut around town, and then go in to rob someone, and then they would go back to a cafe or to a bar and spend the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you help at all as to any definition of these groups; how many were there, how many people were in them, do you know the names of their leaders? That type of thing.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: In the area of our municipality, as far as I heard from members of the Crisis Staff and the police chief, when he used to come, having been invited by the Crisis Staff in order to intervene, two, possibly three, groups had been identified. They had relatively few members, permanent members, let's say. Three to four, they might have had other associates, but leading members were very few in number. One of the group was led by someone called Topalovic. As to whether he was the actual boss ... But I think they were more or less equals. You couldn't really say that one person was bossing everybody else about. Perhaps he was slightly more of a leader than the others. And that group was arrested on the occasion of that intervention that I referred to earlier on. And since there were the four of them and they were arrested, and then another group came along and they released them, they made it possible for them to get out of prison. They threatened the police chief with weapons, they pointed guns at him and they threatened everybody else, and so I suppose that there must have been more than four in the gang. And the chief of police, I suppose, did not dare give us any more details when he came to report on the situation at the War Presidency. I was present because I myself spotted one of those people in the street and I was quite frightened and I came to tell them, and they made jokes at my expense, telling me that I was scared of everything, but then when they received the information from the police chief, they realised how serious the situation is. There was a second group, I think a young guy was a member, but I'm not sure because I only arrived there a couple months earlier and I was more involved in my own work and I didn't really visit the bars or cafes and I didn't really know that many locals, but I know that people would point to others who were involved in such shady dealings. And there was another group, as I said. They had a white Golf vehicle. They had Sarajevo licence plates. They might have stolen the car, I don't know, but apparently they were originally from Petrovac and I know one of them was killed in a car accident. And there were rumours about another group which apparently came from the outside. On occasion they would come and rest, so to say, in Petrovac, about four to five people, and I know that somebody called Caric was a member of that group, and at a later stage he was arrested by the military police. What actually happened to him afterwards, I don't know, but the leadership had told me that he was taken to prison at Kamenica near Drvar, apparently due to some criminal activity on his part. What exactly that criminal activity was I never found out, but when I did ask questions, I was told it wasn't a good idea to ask too many questions about these things. So I know that there were at least three of those groups. As I said, there were not too many people there, but obviously they must have had associates, supporters, and people who may have participated in the division of the booty. There wasn't all that much of it, I suppose, because what could they have found in people's houses? There were not too many wealthy people there --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you again. I'm going to stop you because I'd like to be a little bit more specific. You discussed or mentioned the fact that they robbed people, went into people's homes and stole booty. What other source of crimes did these groups commit?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: As far as I know, some of the robbers at the time - that is to say the first half of 1992 - killed a man whom I knew by sight. He was an attendant at the petrol station and he was killed in armed robbery, and Mr. Jovica Sepa told me about it, and he knew about it because this guy who had been killed was a close friend of his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Stop there, please. What was the ethnicity of the man who was killed at the petrol station, please?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So there was a robbery, there was some murder. Was robbery and this killing directed at people because they were Muslims or was the criminal activity random?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Look, I wouldn't say that those were accidental crimes. Those people were guilty of a succession of crimes. They would run into somebody in the street and relieve them of their car, for example. But the truth is also something else. They normally picked on Muslims because they expected that perhaps this made it less likely for them to be prosecuted. They must have been very surprised when they were arrested, but they robbed anyone. And I think one of the MPs, the one who complained, I think -- well, he had an agricultural holding and some of his flock of animals and -- were taken away and his shepherd was killed as well, and I think they did it out of revenge at a later stage, probably because he was the one who asked for those people to be brought to trial. I don't have any hard and fast facts or information about it, but that was the conclusion drawn across town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have already mentioned in the course of one of your earlier answers the inability of the authorities to deal with these people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, may I first ask a clarifying question to the witness. Mr. Radojko, you said, "They normally picked on Muslims because they expected that perhaps this made it less likely for them to be prosecuted." Could you explain why it was less likely for them to be prosecuted if they would choose Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time the conflict on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina had already started. The Croatian armed forces had crossed over to Brod and a part of the territory was taken all the way to river Ukrina in Derventa. In Herzegovina as well some units had cropped up and started military action. And so there was a great deal of tension. Tensions were mounting and there was a lot of animosity and resentment in the media, through the radio programmes, et cetera. So it was an ongoing thing, and I suppose that, in their frame of mind, that must have concluded that they were allowed to do that, entitled to do that. I don't know what else to say. But at any rate, the reason I'm saying this is that they used to engage in attacks and plundering of Muslim inhabitants rather than Serbs, and Serbs are in the overwhelming majority in the area, so that led me to conclude this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you be a bit more specific as far as the time of that specific incident you mentioned is concerned. Until now you said "beginning of 1992." You now said at that time the conflict had already started. Could you tell us when in the first half of 1992 this incident took place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know a somewhat broader story about this, but it would take up too much time. But I suppose it must have been in June, July, I don't know. At any rate, it was by the middle of the year. I found out about it from that guy who was a member of the Executive Board, and he said that he was sorry that he hadn't done anything himself because he felt that he might have been able to save that man. In other words, that man had offered -- or rather, asked him to take the property that had been looted and keep it at his house, and he said that he couldn't because of the job he had and that everybody would say that he took advantage of Muslims. And he refused them, even though they were friends. And he said, "Had I taken this property, they wouldn't have come and taken it because they wouldn't have had anything." So that's my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have already mentioned in the course of one of your earlier answers about the inability of the authorities to deal with these gangs. Firstly, what did the police try and do?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Well, the authorities were pretty powerless, not altogether powerless. They did have some potential which they did use to some extent, but it was inefficient because those regulations had been inherited from the previous regime and the police administration or the police chief would be at the regional level and the local police was accountable to the regional administration. And that's who gave them their orders, on the basis of which orders they could then act. And there was never anything they had to decide, as such, at the local level. And it was a pretty rigid system which made any efficient and swift reaction impossible. Secondly, as to the armed forces, which had already descended upon Petrovac in large numbers, because there are four regional routes crossing Petrovac in all directions, so it was an area of transit for all military and paramilitary forces, and very often it would happen that, for example, the paramilitaries would enter the town and they would stay at the hotel and they expected to be given everything, full hospitality, and they would pay nothing because they were, so to say, going to war to defend Serbdom. So they had no actual command structure, as such. I knew that the municipal leadership complained because I myself was drafting these documents and these requests addressed to the military command, and the military command would write back saying they were people who had nothing to do with them, and they actually had nothing to do with the actual armed forces. They were the conscripts of the devil. They would join the unit that they picked. They were these paramilitaries. They had some kind of internal command with these smaller groups, but they were not within the framework of the actual system. Sometimes, in order to avoid prosecution, they would declare themselves to be a member of a certain unit and by the time you found out they were not part of that unit, they had disappeared and there was no trace of them, they're at the other end of the country. They were stopped to a certain extent only as late as the end of 1992. Not quite, but to a considerable extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you've mentioned the police, the army. What about the municipal authorities which you were part of? Why didn't you do more to control them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before you continue, I'm totally lost by the previous answer of the witness. You asked him about the inability of the authorities to deal with criminal gangs. First part of the answer the witness explains the ineffective command structures of the police. The second part of his answer is about the presence of military and paramilitary forces and how these paramilitary forces behaved and -- well, a lot more command structures. It's totally unclear what in this respect these -- first of all, from paramilitary forces I would not expect much in investigating criminal gangs. But it's totally unclear how the second part of the answer deals with your question. The first part is clear. Could you please try to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Radojko, you've just mentioned paramilitaries in relation to my question which related to control by the authorities of the gangs. First follow-up question is: What have paramilitaries got to do with control of the gangs?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Based on my knowledge, they were not subordinated to anyone nor could anyone control them. These gangs had taken up the efforts of the few police forces there were, whereas on the other hand the paramilitaries, by the fact that they had passed through the town and acted as they did, they incited the local thieves and local criminals, so to speak, to even engage more in their misconduct. But I wanted to draw your attention to the fact that they -- they were there only temporarily. Most of the local men were on the front line and nobody could have stood up to these people, even if they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the legitimate or regularised and mobilised armed forces; what could they do about it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: As a rule, the mobilised forces were on the front line; however, a good many members of these units were given to abandoning their positions which would, under normal circumstances, be called desertion and would incur criminal responsibility. However, I have to point out that in Bosnia at the time there was no army. These were armed persons who simply joined units. Even those who had not served or had not gone through military service for whatever disability they had, even they joined units. It was only when the situation became too difficult and complicated that they suddenly invoked their disabilities. The local authorities that I worked for had for many times sought, both verbally and in writing, from the military commands that they do something to discipline the soldiers, to prevent the soldiers from taking weapons into town, because there had been victims as a result of members of the army who would appear armed in town, intoxicated, and embark on plundering enterprises, which only added to tensions, escalating them, and nurturing total absence of the rule of law. That was as far as these regular forces could have intervened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, again, time-frame. The witness said: "I have to point out in Bosnia at the time there was no army." What time-frame do we have in mind? Because earlier, talking about the incident, we're talking about June. The witness has testified that there were no military force -- no paramilitary units or -- there. I now do understand that sometimes paramilitary units were there and even encouraged criminal gangs. It's becoming more and more confusing to me. When you said: "At that time there was no army in Bosnia," which moment did you have exactly in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was not my intention to confuse anyone. I simply tried to explain a state of affairs. I used to be a member of an elite military unit and I know what the army looks like. What we Muslims, Serbs, and Croats had was a sort of army which did not really have any command structures, where soldiers could do whatever they wanted. However, officially speaking, these persons were indeed members of the army but they did not behave as such, nor did the command structure have any effective control of them in the sense which a military command structure is, because this person was free to join the unit or leave at leisure. In my opinion and under the then-valid legislation, such conduct should have been punished. Such a situation only served to produce further disorder and lack of discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, yes. How -- could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Hanoteau would have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just would like to understand whether this was only for a time or whether this continued for a longer time and whether this was the general situation. Was there a point in time when this army suddenly became regular and became structured and actually became consistent, you know, actually behaved like what you could expect out of an army? Or you say throughout the conflict it was ongoing and it was always like that, to have this disorganised and disbanded army where everybody was doing whatever they wanted. So what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this situation persisted throughout the war practically; however, the worst situation in those terms was the one in 1992. Back in 1992, nobody knew what they were supposed to do. The officers who had stayed behind, who had not been accepted by the JNA in Belgrade, were felt abandoned and deceived. They were not able to find their way in -- under a new system, whereas there were new members of the army who refused obedience to what they thought were communist officers. It was only after the war that order could be brought to the army. Throughout the war, everyone knew that a unit of a light brigade strength, which was perhaps a battalion of more strength, could simply abandon their positions and go home because they were dissatisfied with the situation. Of course, information about this was suppressed because it was very dangerous for the other side, the enemy side, to know what the situation was like. Now, as far as robberies and general disorder in town was concerned, this showed that the local authorities had no power. Everybody was afraid. Nobody dared to enter a cafe or to try to intervene in any such situation. This is what the situation was like in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but are you just talking about the geographical area that you were in or the entire territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was general disarray in the entire territory. There was no possibility of restoring order. In Banja Luka there was a general unrest, a rebellion. A tank entered the town, and of course the information about this was suppressed because they were afraid the enemy side would find out about it. But in fact there was a putsch effected there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's right, Mr. Radojko, that at least one, if not more, prominent gang members were arrested by the police.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: After the intervention by the MP Milanovic, who went to the municipal building and told the president of the municipality, Novakovic, that he was going to be the first one to move out of town unless the situation is changed, thereupon Mr. Novakovic invited me to keep the minutes of the meeting, and the chiefs of both the military and the civilian police were invited. The public prosecutor was there as well, as were probably some members of the Crisis Staff. Conclusions were adopted at this meeting which were more of a declarative nature, I believe, to the effect that all those responsible should immediately arrest the perpetrators and that the prosecutor should immediately proceed to produce an indictment against them, because the identities of the most prominent gang members were known. I remained by the phone as the duty person throughout the afternoon and the evening. Then the public prosecutor, who could not reach Mr. Novakovic, informed me of the arrest of these persons. I congratulated him on this. The next morning, as I was on my way to work, I saw one of the men leaning against a kiosk there, holding an M-84 machine-gun with ammunition belts, and as I saw him I was shocked and frightened because I was afraid that he would open fire at me. I recognised him. I tried to pass by him inconspicuously because I thought he was going to perhaps recognise me. I knew that this was a dangerous person, and I informed the officials in the municipality that I had seen him, and they were laughing at the fact that I was frightened. Then I asked Mr. Latinovic, the president of the Executive Committee, to call the police chief to double check what the situation was. The police chief said he was going to come over to the municipality building rather than talk over the phone. As he reached the municipal building, he told us that he did not wish to speak over the phone because he believed the phones were tapped. He threw his police cap on the desk as a protest and said that he was no longer going to discharge the duty because they had threatened him with a gun, pointed a gun, put a gun into his mouth. That was the end of that part of the story. The public prosecutor was no longer able to activate the indictment he had written the night before because he did not dare to. There was no police chief anymore, and of course this meant that at that point in time the police would not have been able to act upon the indictment. However, this incident did yield some positive results because later on Mr. Novakovic used his offices to intervene everywhere, including Banja Luka. Mr. Milanovic, who had been thus frightened, and rightly so because later on they had robbed him of his flock of stock and had killed his shepherd, he himself, when he went to the municipal building, said that they had probably done so out of revenge. Still, these gangs seemed to have gone a bit quiet because the -- some of their members had been arrested, after all, and so they lay low for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify -- I'll repeat that. I just want to clarify when this occurred that they were arrested and effectively immediately released.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: This might have been in June, July 1992. I'm not sure. I know that the Muslim population was still there, the majority of them, at any rate. A group of them might have asked to go to Bihac. It was in this period of time. Because of -- and this was because -- exactly because of this criminal conduct expressed in robberies which were done simply because these people thought that they needed these items that they robbed. This was the rule of the Wild West, where the sheriff was powerless in the face of these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I just want to be clear about one other thing, and if this leading is unacceptable, I'll be stopped. You're saying in effect that the chief of police --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is, I'm afraid, clearly an attempt to sum up the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. I have no problem, Your Honour. As you know -- as Your Honour knows, with respect, I've got no difficulty about not leading, it just takes an awfully long time. That's the first attempt, and if that's going to be the reaction, I'm going to be a long time. I've got no difficulty with this, let me make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, that's extremely unfair. Mr. Josse has asked a number of leading questions in the course of this session and this is the first time I've objected. And after the witness has -- only after the witness has been asked, in essence, to encapsulate or summarise a fairly long explanation, and I think it should come from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, I understand that you accept the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, it should not be understood as an invitation by Mr. Tieger to -- not to put leading questions to the witness to the extent he -- as the objection stood, and you'll find out by doing it, as you did before, where the limits approximately are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like you to clarify again, Mr. Radojko, what you were told by the chief of police as to why the men that he was -- that he arrested were -- was released -- were released, perhaps I should say.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: He did not tell me that, he told the leadership. He did not tell me that they were released, but rather that they had been kidnapped from the detention unit in the police station, or rather, that they had been freed by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And any idea how long they were in detention of the police before they were freed by force?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, which is not really reliable - it's difficult to remember these things - at any rate it was already getting dark when I managed to send the copies of the minutes to everyone which stated what they were expected to do. It must have been around 9.00 or 10.00 in the evening. I don't know when it was exactly that they had been freed. Probably during the night or in the early morning hours. I don't know how long it took their associates to get organised for such an action. We did not have a detention unit downtown, and they were supposed to be transferred to Banja Luka directly from the police station. Probably this was why this action ensued so soon, because it is very difficult to pull anyone out of the detention in Banja Luka -- out of the prison facility in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Josse. We'll have a break until quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 90 bis decision has been signed and perhaps even already been filed, but if not then it will be filed this afternoon. Then as far as the transcript, the 92 bis transcript of Mr. Radojko is concerned, it was admitted into evidence by a decision dated the 7th of April, 2004, and I read: "... are admitted into evidence, provided that the witness appears for cross-examination." Then we have a decision of this Chamber which is called "Order relating to Prosecution's applications to admit evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis," which is a decision of the 19th of July, 2004. On the third page it reads: "Considering that the Chamber ..." et cetera, "... has gradually come to the conclusion that the 33 Rule 92 bis witnesses admitted thus far (five of them with cross-examination 6)." Footnote 6 reads: "Another 92 bis witness, Jovica Radojko, who was admitted on the condition that he be cross-examined, was withdrawn by the Prosecution." That means it is in footnote 6 on the record that the witness was withdrawn, which means that no evidence under Rule 92 bis is at this moment before this Chamber. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For what it's worth, it's on that basis and with that knowledge that I had made the assumption that I had alluded to earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's now on the record again where we find it and what procedural course it took.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, I next want to turn to the issue of the departure of the Muslims from your municipality. It might be helpful if I summarise the position with a short leading question. There were three convoys of Muslims that departed; two in 1992 and one in 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The first convoy went in the direction of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Via, in fact -- by crossing the Croatian border?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Which month in 1992 did that convoy leave?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I can't remember. I only remember that I was accompanying the convoy as a negotiator, and there was at least one representative of the Muslims with me. These were people who had long been asking to go to Bihac. I remember that the weather was pinching cold, although I can't date it, really. There are documents somewhere about it. We were assisted by the CzechBat of UNPROFOR. They provided logistics support. There was some exchange involved here as well because the president saw the possibility to allow a certain number of Muslims to leave for Bihac, including -- there were some also inmates who were held in Drnis but some of them had fled. And however, there were the families of these persons who were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm stopping you because I think we can simplify this a little bit. First of all, the Muslims that departed from your municipality, where were they living immediately prior to their departure?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: In Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And were they living freely or were they detained? That's really what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Up until that point, there was no violence, nobody was being detained or anything of the sort. There weren't even tensions, really, not any to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How many people departed in that first convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Only some of them left, those who wanted to. Based on some lists that were drawn up by the Muslim leadership in Bihac and in the general region and by our representatives, there were about 130 to 150 Serbs, some of whom came from this camp near Cazin. The village is there. And some of them were from Bihac town who wanted to cross over to the Serb territory. In order to justify the fact that the Muslims were allowed to leave for Bihac, the president allowed also that some of these people be transferred over there. He also promised that everybody else who wanted to leave would eventually be allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In this convoy of people from your municipality, to what extent did the group include prominent members of the Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: If you mean their leadership, their leaders, as far as I'm concerned, left in secret and they crossed over with the help of Mr. Milanovic and I believe Mr. Ivanic, either in their own cars or I don't know, but they helped them cross over to Bihac. These people, I mean these were normal citizens, and I remember one was an entrepreneur because he, together with my president of the Executive Board, had a private deal which involved the exchange of their property. So they each minded the other's property in Bihac and Petrovac respectively. I only met him a couple of times in my whole life, so I can't remember his name. But at any rate, those were just normal, common citizens. But they had seen that there was risk of further escalation of conflict, and at that stage they asked to be allowed to go. They were probably scared to be found in the wrong place at the wrong time when they might be threatened, and probably they -- most of them wanted to go but our armed forces didn't let them because in the direction, on the road to Bihac, there was a unit made up of Serbs who had already left Bihac. And there was no way you could take that route because they would have shot anyone, and that's why we found a round-about way, going through Croatia, through the then-Republika Srpska Krajina, because the president asked them to cooperate and not make any trouble for us and help that population get out. And since UNPROFOR was there already, they -- I believe -- I don't know who -- what their leadership or our president, they coordinated things with UNPROFOR and made sure they would help them cross the border from the west to the east. And there was this exchange which took place at an area which was manned by the Czech Battalion, and the place is called the Japanese curve. That's where it is, and it is in the area which is now called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear what it's called now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What is that area now called please, Mr. Radojko? The interpreter didn't pick up what you said.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: The area is called the Japanese curve because there is a curve there on the road, a bend, at which there was a car accident and a number of Japanese businessmen were killed there in the accident, and that's why it's called like that. It was the first time I heard the name and I had never heard of it before, even though I travelled down that road pretty often when I was coming back from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how many Serbs did your municipality receive in exchange for the Muslims that left?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Well, approximately as the number of Muslims that left, even more Muslims wanted to leave but the president and the other members of the leadership, because of the pressure that was being brought to bear by those on the front lines, could not allow them to go because the military kept complaining that this was making things more difficult for them, this sort of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There was a second, much larger, convoy in September of 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At that point in time it was -- the situation in your municipality became extremely difficult and dangerous for Muslims. You would accept that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why -- let me rephrase that. What had led to the increase in tensions so that the situation became extremely difficult for them?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I explained this, and it can be found in the transcript. After the first convoy, there were supposed to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. I think "by the transcript" you mean your interview with investigators and lawyers from the Office of the Prosecutor that was held in Banja Luka in the summer of -- June of 19 -- June of 2003, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I mean that too, but I also mean the part of my statement that I've gave before the Court in that same case. But briefly, after that first convoy, since Muslims wanted to go to Bihac, we have to understand the fact that they had family ties to Muslims living in Bihac. And they would have felt safer, since they were more numerous and many of them had property, houses, families there. And in relatively large numbers, I don't know how many, but at any rate many more people than the number of people who managed to cross over wanted to go, even back then, and the president, as far as I know, promised them they would be able to do it but at a later stage when the conditions were more propitious and when there was a little bit less tension with regard to the military. However, the way things developed meant that the military became even worse because the fighting was ever more severe. And I think there was somebody either from the War Presidency or the Crisis Staff - I keep calling it the War Presidency because I don't know at what period of time they had what name - but at any rate, there was this man who was a member of that body, the Crisis Staff or whatever you want to call it, and he said in so many words that there's no possibility of allowing them to go to Bihac, that it couldn't be done. And that's why that kind of transfer was stopped, and so they remained in Petrovac. And so there was this constant threat. The president sent me on a number of occasions to talk to representatives of UNPROFOR and International Red Cross at Lapac, Licko/Petrovo Selo, and Knin, and to ask them to send those people to Split, if possible, if indeed we couldn't send them to Bihac. Initially they accepted, and then afterwards they didn't quite dare go ahead with it and so everything was suspended. Whenever I was travelled with a delegation I was accompanied by two, three respectable Muslim citizens who were the representatives of that Muslim community, and I was both the driver and was in charge of information and talks and everything, so we travelled together as a group, as a single delegation, single unit, as it were. And when that failed and we have told them that there was this risk that in case of further escalation of conflict, the local authorities would not be able to protect the population, because that was the assessment on the part of the president and everybody else. That was their own assessment and, unfortunately, it came true. After an event happened on the battle-field, there was total escalation of conflict and everybody grabbed their rifles and arms and walked up and down town and fired their arms blindly, almost, and they were victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Stop there. It was that event on the battle-field that I was specifically asking you about first of all. Was there an event which made the situation particularly difficult? If so, describe that event briefly.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes, there was one such event in September 1992. Namely, a unit, a Serb unit, mostly made up of people from Petrovac and the refugees from Bihac who, together with their families, came to Petrovac. Well, a lorry was caught in an ambush of a Muslim group, and they killed and massacred people, because it was a swift attack from all sides. And 23 Serb fighters were killed, and I think either 17 or 19 of them were actually originally from Petrovac. It was an odd number and it was less than 20. Anyway, they were taken to the local morgue, to the hospital, and some of the wounded were taken to the hospital as well, because the fighting was still going on.
