And already on that evening the situation became totally horrible. I went to donate blood, and I was attacked by some people there. According to them, the people from the municipality were protecting the Muslims, so I had to flee because they were armed. And mostly there were shots fired all over town. The president convened the meeting on the same evening, tried to find a way out. He phoned everyone left, right, and centre. He phoned the police, but the whole city was on the boil, as it were. And the police people were called. There were guards around houses. To some extent it was successful, but there was simply no possibility of protecting every single household. And so there was some kind of spontaneous revenge underway. And under those circumstances, two or three days later -- that is to say that as the day on the funeral. The funerals probably took place on that evening. And respectable citizens who were Muslims asked for a meeting with the president, and I know that because I was manning the phones all the time. And he somehow, through what channels I don't know, asked them to come at dusk so that they would not be seen, in order to -- for their own safety. And at that stage they found themselves in a very uncomfortable position, and they attended that meeting, and the representative of the military security services from the corps was invited, as well as the chief of police and the commander of the Territorial Defence, and each and every one of them had to report on the situation, and they did that. I know that the TO man complained that his people were being shot at, that actually they were not shot at as such but the shots were being fired in the air and they were being told that everybody knew who they were and their families would be killed. And so those people were a bit reluctant to engage in armed conflict with those groups who were totally out of hand. They were not just robbers anymore but it was a spontaneous kind of movement. There were people who were seeking revenge for the death of their relatives, their brothers, and so on. And so they -- when they came to the meeting and I was taken -- in charge of the minutes, and they turned to the president as some kind of fellow citizen, friend, et cetera, and they called him by his first name. And they said to him: Well, Rajko, brother, what's going on? What is this? This is a shame. Are we meant to be killed in this way? And he felt uncomfortable and he kept apologising. And he said that there was nothing he could do, that he did all he could, but they could see for themselves and they said they did see the guards and that was not sufficient. And the two houses had been set on fire in one part of the town. First they were plundered and then torched, and there were victims, people who had been killed in town. I remember I didn't dare go out on my lunch break on that day, I didn't dare go out of the building. And quite a few people from the town hall felt the same way, because there were shots being fired all over. And somebody was spreading the rumour that Muslims had stayed there thanks to the municipal leadership, and since I myself felt a part of the team, as it were, and I never dared go out because I didn't know that many people, I didn't know what they thought of me, at any rate the news reached us that a woman and a 6-year-old girl were killed, and the situation was horrible. It is simply very difficult for me to describe the way things were and how people who were still in their right minds felt, and especially those who were at the receiving end of all that. Under such circumstances, the president said -- well, on occasion they were involved and on occasion there were only the Crisis Staff people. They were in the hall, outside this delegation, and they were coming in and out, and on the other side there was this meeting of this Serb leadership, and I was sitting at a side table and taking the minutes of the meeting, and those minutes were done in an ad hoc way. I didn't even have a proper notepad. I just had some paper that I had surrendered to the Prosecution on the occasion of the last time that I gave evidence. So basically there was no representative of the military, and in my view, that was the key fact that they had to consider in terms of deciding whether the Muslims could go or not. Because the military guy was the one who was making threats all the time, and that evening he couldn't make it to the meeting because he was somewhere on the battle-field near Bosanska Krupa, together with his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. It might be a good idea just to pause for a moment. There's a lot of information there, and no criticism at all, Mr. Radojko, but you're moving around the issue from one aspect to another quite quickly. Let's go back, if we may, to the approach that you'd begun to describe by various members of the Muslim community to the president of the Municipal Assembly to leave. How did that proceed? How did those negotiations proceed?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I'm certainly not going to be able to give you every single detail. I do appeal to you for some understanding also because a great deal of time has passed, but some things are still etched in my memory. The president of the municipality and all those present from the Serb side had a funny feeling. They were embarrassed, they felt uncomfortable because these things were happening. In the end, I mean, these people used to live together. I wasn't there before, but on the basis of my previous contacts and on the basis of what I had heard, even when some of them had left, some of them were friends, were very close, and in some way the president felt uncomfortable on account of the fact that he could do nothing for them. The only thing he managed to do was to -- well, he simply stopped the meeting and he said we had to help them to get out and that there was no question about it. And then he only asked from the representatives of the military security services to provide guarantees that the army would not attack them as they left and that they would offer assistance. And they promised that they would do that and that they would provide a battalion of military police, basically the entire military police service of the entire corps, in order to ensure the safety of those people when they gathered, to depart, and a part of the way. And he asked the civilian police chief to get in touch with his counterpart in Banja Luka and to explain to him what was happening and that there was no excuse for ignoring it and that people would be held accountable unless they provided proper safety for those people on that morning when they were supposed to leave, because the curfew -- I had forgotten about the curfew. It had already been introduced. They came at dusk and they had to sneak into their own houses and get in touch with their own -- with their own and tell people to try and gather their belongings, et cetera, because there was a request -- for example, they were not allowed to take any valuables with them, any money, any foreign currency, or any jewels, or anything like that, any valuables in general because they were saying, oh, they might provide funding for the war on the basis of that. And then the president said that I would be in charge of their escort and that I would make sure that they had a safe passage. And I said to him that if people were going to be searched for money and valuables, that I wouldn't be able to do that. Even if I had wanted to, I wouldn't be able to do that. And we had to go through enemy territory. Attacks had already taken place there, and one convoy narrowly escaped, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't want to quite go on to the convoy yet. How many Muslims left in that -- in the convoy that you're about to describe, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I think between 2.000 and 2.500. Most probably 2.100 or 200. There was no time to actually count them. There were problems with transport -- there were millions of problems. It was extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to come to transport next. That's -- people left in buses. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: On buses, but there were not enough buses. So some used local trucks owned by the local haulier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And -- because it's 40, 50 vehicles; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Believe me, I have no idea. I set off before everybody got on because I had to go at the head of the convoy with the representatives of the police and make sure that there were no ambushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we come to that in one moment again. What efforts, if any, were made to try and keep the departure of this convoy secret?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Well, everybody who attended that meeting, both the Serbs and the Muslims, agreed that nobody would say a word to anyone, and that's the way it stayed. Plus the Muslims, since they all lived in the same area, the same neighbourhood, and they had to secretly inform their neighbours in the course of the night in order to make it possible for them to prepare for the journey, to get the clothes and valuables or whatever. And as to Serbs, they had to keep silent about it, and that's the way it was. And a sign was agreed on the basis of which we would gather very quickly so that the local Serbs wouldn't find out about it in order to avoid anyone deciding to attack them, because all that was the consequence of this revenge. So it was agreed that at 6.00 in the morning the police car would -- there would be the police call for people to gather. And that's what happened, and within a short period of time they came to the agreed spot. And the police was already there, the civilian police, and some from the military police as well. And it's a rather large area, large square, which is surrounded by more or less two rows of police officers, soldiers, I don't know who else was there, they were fully armed, and they kept guard. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You went off, as you've already told us, at the front of this convoy. How far in front of the first vehicle carrying these departing people were you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I don't know; a couple of hundred metres, 500 metres. At any rate, we tried to keep some kind of visual control and contact so as for the convoy to stay together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We haven't discussed and I haven't asked you about the direction in which this convoy left. There's no dispute, I'm sure, it went towards Travnik, in Central Bosnia. Why didn't it go to Bihac? Why did it go to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Precisely for the reasons I've already mentioned: Those people didn't want to go to Travnik; they were made to go there because the circumstances made it necessary for us to take them there. They wished to go to Bihac, and afterwards, as far as I can tell since the fighting in Bihac intensified and they would have been mobilised straight away and sent into battle, when there was the possibility of talking to UNPROFOR, they actually would have preferred to go to Split because they discovered that from Split they would have been able to go to other Western countries and escape the war. But it wasn't possible, due to the circumstances, so they went there against their will because they were mobilised there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At some point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one question. You said they wanted to go in this direction, that direction was all not possible. "... so they went there against their will because they were mobilised there as well." Why did they have to go there? Why couldn't they -- if they did not want to go into the direction in which they were taken, why not leave them where they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely for the reason that the situation had become untenable. The president told them openly that he was unable to guarantee their safety any longer, that he was doing all he could, but there were those attacks still taking place and there were victims. And for some time already prior to that he had tried to make it possible for them to leave, but since in the direction of Split UNPROFOR didn't allow for that, when I went together with the Muslim delegation, I mean we went as a single delegation, to speak to them, they told us openly when they gave up the idea of helping us with this journey. I don't remember whether those people were from UNPROFOR or from the Red Cross, but at any rate one of those people said that their head office considers this type of departure of the population as ethnic cleansing. That was the first time that I heard the term "ethnic cleansing." I didn't know, I found out later what it was all about. And they said -- when I said that the local authorities had no powers over the police and that they would never have any powers over the military command and that we were powerless, they said that it was our problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me stop you. And then did they say: We want to go? Or did you say: There's no other way out than to go? I mean, I asked you: Why not leave them where they were? And you said: Well, the situation had become untenable and the president had told them openly that he -- that's all -- did they then say: We, nevertheless, want go? Or did they say: We'd like to stay in the cellars of our houses and we'll see what happens? I mean, who finally said: Let's get on the bus and let's move out? Who finally took that decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They came up with the request to leave right at the start. They came with this request, and I mean the respectable citizens representing the Muslim community. They had been requesting to leave for months, but the president could not allow them to leave because the other side had openly been threatening and saying that nothing of the sort should be allowed. This is, of course, an interpretation of mine. I'm afraid that this other side wanted them to stay behind as sort of hostages, because they kept saying that women and children were free to leave while the military-age men were to be left behind. But something of the sort could not be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not? Why could women and children not leave as they wished? Are they not -- are they not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That wasn't the way the people wanted to leave. They stated openly that they did not wish to be separated from their families. And I think that they were right in insisting on this because there was a far greater danger in leaving the able-bodied men behind because they would indeed be left as sort of hostages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why would they be hostages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of all the things happening on the front line and they were in an encirclement. Well, ultimately, that was the way they felt, at any rate, and they stated that they did not wish to stay behind. They said that if their families were leaving, they would leave, too. You see, this was one of the options that the president had presented them with at this meeting. It was solely on this request of theirs that the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll go into further details perhaps at a later stage. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've got to the point in time where the convoy departed. You were at the front of it. You were with a police officer, is that correct? A police commander, I think.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Kljuc, you learnt that the convoy had been attacked. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What information did you learn in Kljuc about this attack and from what source did you receive this information?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Directly from the people there. When we arrived in Kljuc, we realised that our column, the column behind us, consisted of only three to four buses. We realised this as we were passing a curve. That's why we stopped at Kljuc, waiting for the others to come up. As the others were coming up, somebody told us that the convoy had come under attack, the latter part of the convoy. Shots were fired, and that perhaps there were even people wounded. I went to the rear of the convoy, asking whether anyone was wounded, and they told me that there was somebody wounded in a truck somewhere. I later found out that a boy was, in fact, killed and that several persons were wounded. I told them that they would be given medical assistance. I got into a car and hurried to the hospital there because I was in charge of logistics. I got some medical staff there and an ambulance and went to that section of the convoy where the wounded were. Unfortunately, the boy was already -- the young man was already dead, but there were several wounded who -- in fact, one of them was taken back to Petrovac and I don't know what happened to him later on. At this stage, I didn't know whether there were any other persons injured. I was told that there were none, but they told me that there was one truck, the tires of which had been punctured, and it stayed somewhere behind. Since the column had stopped at a curve, I said that we should move on because it was a dangerous position, and I said that we should keep on moving until we went past Kljuc at a point where we would meet again. When we met up there, I went down the convoy and realised that there were more people wounded. I agreed with the commander, the police commander, that several police officers were to go to a cafe in a village nearby to simply see whether there was any danger lurking there, as a sort of reconnaissance. As soon as they returned, they told us to leave the place immediately, and we asked why. They said that once the people in the cafe found out that we were heading from Petrovac, that they said that they were going to take up arms. That's why the convoy started moving again, and this police commander, who was in fact an ad hoc commander, had two cars of police officers. One of the police cars went at the rear of the column to wait for the truck that had been left behind, dragging behind, and the column proceeded, whereas I went to the hospital to make sure that the wounded were medically treated. So the other police car was at the head of the column. We agreed at which location near Mrkonjic we would stop which was appropriate. There, as we reached this particular site, we met up with a medical vehicle who had come to take care of the wounded. However, the Muslims who were in these vehicles told us that the wounded did not wish to stay in the Mrkonjic hospital, but rather that they only wished medical supplies -- to be given medical supplies, because apparently there were some medical staff among them. The ambulance that was there gave them whatever medical supplies they had, and they said that this was enough for them and that we could resume our journey. We continued the journey up until Knezevo where the army took over. The army took over from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as far as you know from information you subsequently received, the convoy then did proceed without further attack into Muslim-held territory?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. There were no further attacks. We hurried through the territory -- across the territory, and I don't believe anybody was aware of us passing through there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And let's just be clear about this in relation to the questions that the learned Presiding Judge asked you: There was no international assistance whatsoever in relation to this particular exodus.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: There was none.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The third convoy was in the early part of 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes, that's correct. It was wintertime. I believe it was in February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And very brief questions about that. How many people were in that convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Perhaps 150, 200, 240. Let's say from 150 to 240. I can't give you the exact number. I wasn't escorting the vehicles or anything of the sort, so I don't know how many had been ordered. I was only tasked with making sure that they reach their destination and to negotiate with the authorities there on behalf of the municipality that we would take care of food and -- or rather, that we would cover the expenses entailed by the food and accommodation given to them, and that they not be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In which direction did this convoy go?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: It went to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do you know why these 150 or so Muslims left at that particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I do. Because of the fact that this second convoy had departed so suddenly and these people resided in rural areas, not in towns, it was impossible to organise their departure swiftly. And in order to make sure that the bulk of the people leave, they -- these people were not even informed of the convoy. And the -- these persons lived in mixed villages, where there were both Serbs and Muslims residing, and they had their village guards which kept them safe. There were no attacks against them. In order not to jeopardise the departure of this other large group of people, for whom there was risk of attack, these other people were not even notified of the possibility for departure, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to briefly return to the second convoy, the one that you've described in some detail. I forgot to ask you about what happened to the homes and property of the departing Muslims. Please tell the Chamber about that.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Their houses and property were left behind. When it was agreed that they should leave, and I had already relayed the views presented by the Red Cross and UNPROFOR to the president, who had known of these positions even before from his own contacts, I told him that the municipality was in charge of the property of all these people and that these people had -- were entitled to indemnity in case their property was damaged. That's why I told them to tell the people at the meeting that whoever wanted to leave should lock up their homes and outbuildings and to hand the keys over to the municipal officials before their departure in order to make up a list of the properties and in order for these properties to be listed. The following morning -- and for the property to be sealed. The next morning the municipal officials were collecting the keys, and in cases where the keys were not brought over to them, they were told that the keys were waiting for them at the property themselves. After that, they started touring these properties and making up lists of all the items left and sealing all these houses. They itemised all the belongings in order for everyone to know what had been left behind and to prevent the indemnities being asked for items that had not been, in fact, left behind. Since refugees had been streaming into the area from all sides, some of the properties were given to them to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to assist with what percentage were used and what percentage remained sealed and unused?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: In the beginning, all the properties were sealed. At a later stage, a certain percentage -- or rather, almost all of them were given over to the refugees because 4 to 5.000 refugees came from Bihac. They were staying at their relatives' or at their friends'. They were even put up in some public buildings, and most of these properties were given to these refugees. There were other refugees from Central Bosnia that streamed into the area. Several houses were occupied by the local residents, who were not entitled to do that, and I know that there were some difficulties with them, that there were cases when these people were evicted from such houses. I was not, myself, involved directly in the paperwork but I know of such instances. Therefore, it was refugees, for the most part, who occupied these properties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, isn't it true that one of the core issues in this respect would be whether proper care was taken of the property, immovable and movable, of those who left or whether a different course of action was taken, such a course of action as, for example, described in Prosecution Exhibits 748, tab 9? I mean, isn't that the core of the issue, and whether the keys were given in the morning or the afternoon, isn't it true that why the keys were given is the core issue? We hear a lot of evidence, a lot of details, which is rather irrelevant if the core issue has not been dealt with. I'm using these words and I'm referring to this exhibit because I think I can do that in the presence of the witness who might not know all the P exhibit numbers by heart, but I take it that you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do, but I'm unable to take this matter any further at this stage. Would Your Honour give me one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- I'm going to move on. If Your Honour wishes to pursue that matter, then of course it's a matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it will be done in cross-examination. I -- I mean, it's part of the evidence that is in front of us. But we spent a lot of time where the core issue is not dealt with, and, Mr. Josse, if the core issue, on the basis of the information we get, goes to the favour of those who left -- in favour of what could have asked in two or three questions, which is: Those who left, did they still own their property? What was done with it? And then let's forgot about keys to be given in the morning or the afternoon or what else do we have on whether there were even a few people who illegally occupied that other -- I mean, this case is not about whether some individuals may have taken some of the -- may have occupied some of the property at a certain moment. The core issue is before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I've already gone this far. I'm not able to cross-examine my own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do understand. I do understand. And at the same time, of course, that's the question that the Chamber finds at the core of -- of this matter. If you say: Let's then wait, what happens, but spend not too much time on details which are irrelevant if the core issue is not clear. I'm not saying that they could be relevant once we have a better view on the core issue, but the main questions are not yet put to the witness, and perhaps we should then wait, Mr. Josse, perhaps in re-examination that you would deal with the matter further to that extent at that moment relevant. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to move to a different topic altogether, please, Mr. Radojko, and that relates to the degree to which you recall the municipality complaining to the republican government in Pale about the activities of these gangs. Did you communicate with Pale in any way?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: At that time, the communications with Pale went mostly through MPs, people who went over there, and in writing. The telephone lines were functioning on occasion. I know that the president of the municipality would use the lines whenever possible, but then one or two or three days would pass with the lines being down. That's why we could not rely on the telephone lines and neither could they. On several occasions in this period of time and later, some documents were dispatched, mostly to Banja Luka because that's where the security centre of the police was located, and requests were sent to the 2nd Corps command which was, in actual fact, located in our area. All of us at the municipality felt, as citizens, that there was a lack of order in many aspects and the local leadership oftentimes made decisions asking that certain shortcomings or deficiencies be rectified, that the police or the military command, depending on whose members were wreaking havoc throughout town, that they take these matters into their hands. I remember that a member of the Assembly himself asked that something be done by -- about the fact that armed people were entering town, that the military commands take care of this. I recall, for instance, that soldiers would go to the cafes in the town because their unit was deployed near, and they also drove up in a tank once. They would open fire from their arms indiscriminately. There were such requests put forth, and as a result of these requests, steps were taken and the situation was rectified, although there was disorder in this particular point in time. We used a round-about way to ask from the police station, which is only 1 kilometre from the municipal building -- so we could not ask anything from them directly. We had to go through Banja Luka to send any requests we had, and it took a day, whereas it should have taken an hour. The president would sometimes phone the police chief, who was a professional police officer, and I know that he himself had to deal with any order that the police administration had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, time-frame for question and answer, could you assist me, together with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, yes, I clearly need to break this down in a number of ways, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it's time for a break anyhow, so that gives you some time to further -- if there are -- if there's anything else, I would like to have a break to start within the next two to seven minutes. I'm certain that you'll find a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to be a little bit more specific about this, if we may, Mr. Radojko. Did you personally write any memos or letters to the republican leadership?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: About how many and at what period of time did you do that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Throughout the time period I spent there as a civil servant, I recall that I wrote 30 to 40 different memos to the superior bodies, and this is in this four- to five-years period. These were official letters sent to competent bodies in a given field, be it education, health care, army, administration ministry, ministry of the police. Some letters were sent to the then-president of Republika Srpska. We mostly sent different requests to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In 1992, how did these communications get to Pale? How were they sent there?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I don't recall that it was possible to send letters by mail. It had to be taken by a courier or, rather, whoever was going to Pale, a functionary, an MP, they would take letters along. If there was someone headed for Banja Luka, then this person would take whatever mail was there for Banja Luka. Or, it would be sent through coded mail by the communications centre. I don't recall anything being sent by ordinary mail, as is done in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be a convenient moment, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break until ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've just told us about how you communicated in 1992 with Pale. Did you ever get a response in that year?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Well, in relation to these events there wasn't much communications with Pale. We mostly addressed the Banja Luka centre and the military command, which was initially in Drvar and later on in Sibelj [phoen]. In the later period, there weren't any responses or reactions, really, from Pale that would have been helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I think when we are talking about communication responses, whether they're helpful or not, a really totally different subject. Do you understand my problem with your answer? The answer is about whether you could communicate with Pale -- I take it at least, Mr. Josse, that you're talking about the technical possibility of communicating, or were you asking about the content of the communications?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I was content with the answer, but if Your Honour is not, I understand, and Your Honour can pursue the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour looks at me to pursue it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm trying to understand what you want to learn from the witness. Is this about what the communications, as far as subject is concerned, were about or whether there was a possibility to communicate? On one of the earlier questions that was questioned just before the break, the witness said to us that 30 to 40 communications in writing in five years, so that's an average of six to eight a year, on many subjects. When I heard the answer and when I heard the question, I thought: Are we going to learn anything about what was in this communication or are you seeking to establish whether there was technical possibilities for communications at all? Now your question was: Did you get a response? There again, are you seeking to know what the response is? Then of course we would know what the question had been so that we are talking about the content of the communication, or were you interested to know whether it was at all possible to give a response? And then the witness says that he mainly addressed Banja Luka but in the later period there weren't any responses or reactions. We still don't know whether from Pale -- oh, yes, he says from Pale. But there were no responses or reactions that would be been helpful. That leaves a complete mystery of why it was not helpful. If it was about medical care, whether they could not provide any additional beds. It's totally -- I don't know what to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't want to spend any more time on the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I want to let you know why I'm puzzled, both by answers and the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for so informing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, I want to ask you some specific matters. Really two issues. The first is the unlawfulness and the picture that you painted of the Wild West in Petrovac. Did you or any of your colleagues inform Pale of the situation in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I myself was not authorised to do so, and had I tried to do that it would have been considered as overstepping my authority. That was not part of my duties; however, I do not know that MP Milanovic talked about the unlawfulness in the circles he frequented, and certain steps were taken both by the army and the police. The situation gradually was brought under control because I know that some of the groups that had initially been wreaking havoc in town were, in fact, mobilised. I don't know whether it was forcibly or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, the question was whether you informed Pale or whether one of your colleagues did so. The answer, apparently, is: No, I didn't. Whether you think you couldn't, that's another matter. And what I understand, you do not know whether Mr. Milanovic, I took that for an answer that you did not know whether any other person --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't entirely understand that, frankly, and I assume it should read "I do not know whether MP Milanovic --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood it. It could have been clarified. We could have interrupted it. Then you start talking about whether the situation improved. The issue at this moment is communication with Pale on the problems. So let's keep it to that. And, Mr. Josse, you're invited also to keep strict control that as soon as we move out of where -- what apparently the relevance of your questions is, let's try to focus entirely on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That, with respect, I entirely agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radojko, these are very specific issues I'm asking about. You state you didn't contact the republican authorities because it wasn't within your remit. Were you aware as to whether anyone else did?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: As far as I know, Milanovic relayed Mr. Novakovic's requests on these matters. I know this from the conversations the two of them had. In what form the request was in fact relayed and what its substance was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Specifically I now want to ask you about the convoys that departed, and in particular the second convoy of in excess of 2.000 people. As far as you are aware, was there any communication with Pale about that departure?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Not on the departure -- or rather, at the point of departure. When we returned to Petrovac after having escorted the convoy part way, Mr. Novakovic told me that the then-President Karadzic had contacted him on this issue. He told me that the conversation had taken place at the time we were roughly in Knezevo and that Karadzic had raised his voice at him, that he had criticised him strongly for the fact the people were relocated and that Novakovic replied by saying that he could do nothing more about it, that he could not protect the population adequately. I don't know whether this was the motive why they had contacted each other, but as I -- as far as I was told, this was what they talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea why Mr. Karadzic took the stance that he did?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand Novakovic's reaction, his -- he reacted negatively because already at the time there were stories of ethnic cleansing going on and he wished to put a stop to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In general, were there communications that you were aware of between Mr. Novakovic and Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: There were exchanges of information, although I don't know of what nature. I know that whenever Mr. Novakovic was able to get hold of him over the phone when the lines were on, he talked to him. I don't know what they discussed. I sometimes happened to be in the office when they spoke over the phone, but I would then leave the room out of discretion. I know that they had contacts but I don't know what on exactly. Novakovic did not hesitate to contact him, although he was a person of authority. But he did not feel any reservations in getting in touch with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There was a general story, or joke, in circulation about Pale and the type of ministers who were accepted into the government in Pale and the distance of Pale from the rest of the Republika Srpska. Perhaps you could tell the Chamber that joke or that story.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes, I can. In our contacts with the government at Pale, we realised that they were more confused than we were and were unable to understand our problems. I told this as a joke to a circle of persons I was able to tell that at the time. I told them that the government was at a military check-point between Sarajevo and Pale and that people who were felt to have the necessary professional qualifications were invited to become members of the government as they were fleeing Sarajevo. We simply did not receive the instructions or assistance of the kind one would expect to receive from ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What would -- do you say, Mr. Radojko, to the suggestion that the lawlessness in your municipality that you have described was inspired by the Pale administration?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Well, perhaps this would, to a certain extent, clear the faces of our municipal authorities if this were indeed the case; however, not even at the beginning or later on, when the situation improved, did the municipal authorities have any impact on the events. They wanted to have a positive impact on the situation but could not even have impact on the negative -- on escalating the negative impact. They could not have the police arrest the perpetrators. They could not make the prosecutor's office prosecute those that were arrested by the police. There was the general inertia of the state authorities. They did do something. I remember the Crisis Staff asked that the police make a list of all the persons who were known to steal the property of the Muslims. I believe that some of the names were listed and such reports can be found in the Petrovac files. So they were doing something but -- for instance, if you found a person stealing someone's property, they would be taken into custody, but the prosecutor's office would not issue an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've stopped you because you have just described --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've stopped you because you have just described what was wrong with the local administration. What I was asking you about was the Pale administration. It's the Prosecution case, Mr. Radojko, that the violence that you have described was inspired by people in Pale. What do you say to that proposition?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: It was not inspired by them because they were unable to control the situation back in their court. I can give you a few examples. They appointed completely incompetent persons to some positions, like the general director of the commodity reserve agency, where in, my contacts with him, I realised that the man was a wall painter by profession. I also recall instances when the property from Tas was seized. The story went around that whoever wanted to get hold of the property there would simply go over there and take what they liked. Well -- and you can judge what they were able to do by taking a look at what they were able to assist us with. Many people liked the fact that they were able to formally hold high positions but were in fact lacking any qualifications for the job they did. I recall that many of the ministers had not even passed the official state exam.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Prosecution for that position is that the lawlessness you've described was condoned by the authorities in Pale. What do you say to that proposition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Josse can ask questions to the witness without attempting to characterise the Prosecution's position one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think he could do that at the same time. I do not hear you say that he's presenting -- he may have carefully listened to the Prosecution's position falsely, and it certainly speeds up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I have no objection to the questions. It's just that I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at the same time, Mr. Josse, if you phrase the question: If someone would say ... and then you exactly formulate the Prosecution's position, then the matter's clear enough and the witness is not confronted with the fact that this is the Prosecution's position. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, did the Pale administration condone the lawlessness that you have described in such detail?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: When I think back about that period, I don't think that they condoned what was happening. I know that we were asking them to rectify the situation, and eventually they did. I'm simply telling you that they did not have quality mechanisms enabling them to react swiftly. Rather, the -- it took a long time for the information to reach a point; it would always take a round-about way. And the situation we found ourselves in was difficult. In short, no, they did not lend any support to such behaviour. Rather, they supported the requests that we put forth to them, and this is something you can see for yourselves from correspondence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I haven't seen any specific correspondence. If there's any, the Chamber, of course, is very much interested because in this testimony no document whatsoever, whereas there seem to exist a lot, has been presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are a lot of documents in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But not presented yet through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have presented none through this witness; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would have a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your reply, sir, you mentioned you were not inspired of them because they were able to control the situation back in their court. [In English] "I can give you a few examples. They appointed completely incompetent persons to some positions, like the general director," and so on. [Interpretation] What is your explanation of this state of affairs? Why -- how can you explain this -- managed so badly -- administration so bad. Why were there appointments of incompetent persons made? When you say "they appointed --" "they appointed incompetent persons." When you say that, what do you mean? Who were these persons who were appointed? Who were in charge of these appointments, and for what reason -- why was their administration so bad?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps we should check, Your Honour. There's clearly a problem there. We were getting -- the translators were translating in the alternative one after the other. The learned Judge, Judge Hanoteau, wouldn't know that because clearly he was speaking in French. Perhaps we can just check what was happening. That's very clear on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not entirely clear to me, but if there's any confusion, perhaps you can repeat the question, Judge Hanoteau, although it was a long one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Save for the fact of course I assume in B/C/S it wasn't a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I listen with one ear in French, and with the other I listen to the English translation. I did not hear, apart from always minor choices interpreters have to make, I did hear any major problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For what it's worth, I had the impression that the interpreters were assisting or supplementing each other. Maybe speaking with them would clarify that that was or was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm sorry for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did the witness understand my question? That's the most important thing. Did you understand my question, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Your Honour. If you allow me, I'd like to try and answer. It is the Assembly that is responsible for the appointment of the ministers; however, for the appointment of all the other staff charged with operative duties, it is the government or individual ministries who are responsible for appointing them. The same situation exists today. Now, I'll give you my opinion why they were felt to be incompetent. First of all, they were completely isolated up there at Pale in all the different senses. Most of the people over there never visited our areas, never came to ask us directly what sort of problems we were experiencing and how they could be remedied. They seemed to be operating as an end unto themselves. As for the staffing issue, they simply appointed persons who were within reach. As these persons were not familiar with the operation of the state administration and the government, they tried to recruit other people from other areas of the country who had the necessary expertise. A large percentage of the government at the time was made up of physicians who, of course, have no knowledge of how a government should operate in wartime. It started out chaotically and continued so. In -- under such circumstances in the absence of qualified persons who would take positions and steps, the chaos spread out into the lower institutions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but within these incompetent persons, do you include the accused and Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not saying the accused was incompetent, because the way he presided over the Assembly at the time when it was still a joint Assembly, and later on, was professional, as far as I was able to glean by watching Assembly sessions on TV. He -- his name was never raised in these discussions that I'm dealing with just now. Nobody mentioned his name or his role. Up until 1994 or 1995, he was the president of the Assembly, nothing more. He had no special authority nor was mentioned as a person of particular significance back in our area. Only in 1994 when Serbia introduced a blockade on the import of some goods did he start saying, as far as I recall - and I'm talking about the accused - that we should try to obtain some of the staple food that we lacked in our area through the accused. It was only in this context that he was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you were saying that the Assembly was in charge of appointing the ministers and the -- and if I understood you right, you said that the ministers were not competent. So Mr. Krajisnik being the president of that Assembly, did you think that he was involved somehow in the appointment of these incompetent persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have understood your question. You probably are drawing the conclusion that the speaker of the Assembly can't be competent if the ministers are incompetent. Let me explain. As the speaker, he had the same role as the speaker in the UK parliament, for example, and as such, he had one vote. In that Assembly where, I don't know, except for one or two members, everybody else was from the SDS party. And there were lots of rival groupings within the SDS itself. It was not a fully developed party with a fully developed party structure; it was just a movement. Many people, even in that period of time, had to be thrown out of the party because of their dishonourable behaviour, at least in our area, and basically because they were criminals. And for these reasons, on the basis of what I saw on television, those broadcasts which were live broadcasts, I'm drawing the conclusion that he as a person, as an engineer or an economist, I don't know, that he's -- he was pretty skilled at his job. But as to ministers, very often different factions would support their man and very many of them were totally incompetent. If I think back, for example, very often key ministers were being switched. The minister for police and army matters was switched in the middle of the war. On the other hand, I myself participated in -- in a meeting at which the defence minister attended and the military representatives wouldn't even say hello to him. So that was the situation. It was all kept hidden in order to prevent people from getting too frightened and running away, as it were. But everybody else, the people who were in the know, as it were, knew about it. There was a great deal of intolerance amongst different factions. I'm not going to say it was outright hatred, but it wasn't good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, if I may. When you were in your municipality during this war period, if there had been a competent government, what would you have expected from a competent government? How could things have turned out otherwise had the government been competent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that period of time it was very difficult to improve the situation. The state was falling apart and the professional members of the military were not in favour of anyone in the beginning. Obviously they had sympathies for their own ethnic groups and that's how they joined their national armies, but most of them, the overwhelming majority, who were honourable men, the never allowed for crimes to happen. I do remember at the beginning of the war I saw a soldier who actually stole somebody's TV set, and he was shot on the spot. I saw his dead body; I was passing by. Unfortunately, those officers as well were scattered all over the place wherein many of them were from Serbia and other republics, and they went back home. And those who remained were not very numerous and many of them felt that they were in some way condemned to stay there and they were unhappy that they had nowhere else to go. On the other hand, the civilian authorities did not really accept them as such, did not really have any understanding for them. They were deprived of their property, of their real estate, of their flats that they had back in Slovenia, in Croatia or whatever, so there was a general state of disorderliness and a lot of ignorance. Supposedly, probably, presumably something could have been changed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in your municipality, what did you expect from the Pale government had it been competent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We, to be honest, did not expect a great deal. We made do as we best could, but it would have been realistic to expect for the police powers to function at the local level, the immediate level, because we had difficulty even communicating with Banja Luka at the time, let alone Pale. It would have been realistic to expect that there would be a minister who would have been able to understand that police had to react on the spot. Secondly, something else that would have been useful had it been done back then: For the military commanders, for some kind of regulation to have been passed, in order for the people who had been caught stealing to be arrested and to do forced labour or have a penitentiary unit or whatever and that they would not be allowed to go home until the end of the war. So those things were the things that we asked for, requested them, very firmly. I know the president asked for it very firmly. I don't know whether he did it in writing or not. I suppose there must have been something in writing. I don't know whether he used exactly the same language as I'm using now, but we tried to choose the best possible way of putting this to the leadership, et cetera. But had these two things been done on time, presumably all the bad things would have been less. Unfortunately, for example, the armed forces -- I mean, we had understanding for those reasons as well, but the armed forces wanted to direct and manage everything during the war. They asked for the command posts to be created in our area. They came in and they asked for it, but legally speaking it was impossible. It wasn't a place that they had freed or liberated in any way, and it wasn't a place where there were no authorities either, but the president didn't allow for that to happen and I said that I would personally run away from any place which was managed and governed by the army. And that's when the first conflicts started to happen between the local authorities and the military command, and this kind of conflict went on until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, did you in 1992 receive any order from Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact, did you receive any communication from him?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And are you aware of any communication from him to any other member of the municipal authority?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: No, not at that time. He had no communication with our representatives. Perhaps with Milanovic when they met at the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn briefly, please, to the departure of the Serbs from your municipality. When did the Serbs leave Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: In September 1995, on the 14th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did they leave?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Well, they fled. They fled before the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as far as you're aware, have many -- any Serbs returned once peace was established?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I don't know how many exactly returned. Quite a few people registered because they wanted to regulate property matters, et cetera, and they got their IDs, local IDs for that reason. But those people don't actually live there. They live on the territory of the Republika Srpska. Most of them live in Republika Srpska, in Banja Luka and its surroundings, and some of them in Derventa and other places. Some of them returned to that area of the municipality, Petrovac, that went to the Republika Srpska, and that's the area towards which many people gravitate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to take you back in time and ask you about something that I failed to deal with much earlier. Could you have a look at this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Variant A and B document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before you look at that -- leave that to one side, please, would you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko -- Mr. Radojko, Mr. Josse is asking you to put the document, for a minute, aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I should have asked you this: When the Serbs left Petrovac, did all the Serbs leave?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: All those who managed to flee did so. A certain number of them had not managed to do that, either because they were elderly or disabled or lived in out-of-the-way places and nobody informed them that they should leave, so they stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what happened to those Serbs who remained?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: Well, all Serbs who remained were either killed, and mostly massacred, even though we're talking about the elderly or those who were psychiatric patients, so they didn't even know what was going on. And some of them who lived in outlying villages were either killed or were brought to the prison in Petrovac and they were exchanged as war prisoners in 1996. That was a smallish group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, is there any documentation about this, as we have lots of documentations about other massacres or mass killings, so that we get an impression of the numbers we are talking about? And I'm also addressing the Prosecution to ask whether there is any documentation which would then be exculpatory material? That's a thing for --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness testified about a later period in time where Serbs had to flee the municipality, or at least major part of the municipality, and that those who remained were either killed and mostly massacred. Is there any documentation on -- well, reports on numbers or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There may be, Your Honour, but it's not something to which the Prosecution has directed its attention to my knowledge, and I certainly can't -- you mention exculpatory information, and I can't see any way in which that would be -- have an exculpatory component in the context of this case. I -- I didn't object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the whole of the balance --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't object to the questions because the Defence has previously said that they were interested in eliciting some forms as contextual or background information, and I leave that to them in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you for not having focussed. I just wonder -- first of all, I address Mr. Josse because he put the question to the witness, but Mr. Josse might not have exactly the same resources, and if such material would be there -- Mr. Josse, have you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, I have got no material in relation to this whatsoever. The best the Chamber can do is to ask the witness. I ask Your Honour to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we could ask you. Mr. Radojko, you told us about those who had remained in the municipalities where most of the Serbs had fled at a later stage, that they were killed and that -- massacred. Is there any report known to you about this specific -- was it at one day? Was it during a couple of weeks? Was it -- how many victims were there? Were there 20? Were there 200? Were there 2.000? Are you aware of any such specific report on your municipality? Not general reports, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our municipality no longer exists. There's nobody doing any official research on this, but I talked to people from those parts. My aunt was taken prisoner and she was exchanged, and she was 78 years old at the time, and she was not very mobile, to be honest, but she was exchanged as a POW. I talked to a man who was from the same village as my father-in-law. He had been tortured, his feet were smashed, and he was made to stand barefoot and then his toes were broken by a rifle-butt, and he was taken a month after Petrovac was taken by the other side. And his name was Niko something. I can't remember his family name. He's from the village of Risovac. And apart from that, talking to people in Banja Luka, I obtained information that through those associations and organisations of the families of the missing, et cetera. They obtained data about several dozens of people killed in that way, and there were not many more. There were not too many people there. The entire municipality of Petrovac must have had about 15.000 people, and basically all those who were left behind -- I mean, they were not allowed to stay at home. They were either killed or deported to prisons or camps, and basically they were deported. For this reason, the rest of the population was basically on the run, because there's a very negative overall context when those self-same Muslims perpetrated genocide in that area. I don't know whether you're aware of it, but in the area of the Kladusa municipality, according to the census from 1991, there was 80 per cent of Serbs, 40 per cent in Bihac, Bosanska Krupa 70-something per cent, and Sasin was the only area in which Muslims were in the majority because they were about 40 to 42 per cent of Serbs. After World War II, Serbs were either in the minority or didn't exist in that area. According to the census from 1991, there are also no Serbs in Kladusa or Sasin and it is a municipality of 60.000 inhabitants, and so on and so forth, and this is the reasons why these people were on the run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was not my question, but nevertheless could you please -- you referred to the earlier census, where you said the area of Kladusa, 80 per cent Serbs, and then you referred to 1991, but that must be a mistake, I take it, because later on you referred to the 1991 census. Could you tell us, what was the first census you referred to, what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour, perhaps I didn't quite make myself clear. The first census where there is a clear Serb majority was before World War II. After the genocide which took place in World War II, and then there is the other set of data where there are next to no Serbs, and it is for this reason that those tensions existed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I just asked you to correct what reads as "1991." Now you say it's the census from before the Second World War. You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 1931, is that right, Mr. Radojko, rather than 1991? Is that right, Mr. Radojko?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: I apologise, I still haven't made myself clear, I suppose. The first set of data refers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Radojko, you have made yourself perfectly clear. The first set of data was before the Second World War, and whether that was 1931 or 1935 is not of great importance at this moment. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want now to turn to the document that you have in front of you, please, Mr. Radojko. That is the document known in this court as the Variant A and B document. I'll be stopped if there's any objection to my leading on this. When you were interviewed by investigators and lawyers -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I was just anticipating, but since counsel's already stopped, I think he's about to -- this is clearly about to be a leading question and I don't think leading in this area is appropriate, and he can proceed to ask the questions, in my judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When did you first see the document, Mr. Radojko?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I saw it on the occasion of giving evidence in another case, I believe 2003. I said on that occasion that notwithstanding the fact that I was only seeing the document at that stage, I did remember references to that, but most of it had never been implemented. I do remember that case. I'm not going to go through this in any great details so as not to waste anyone's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That would suffice for my purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could Your Honour give me a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, unless you would think that the first of your series of questions could not be completed in the next seven minutes, I would like to invite you to start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to be hard-pressed to be prepared to begin tomorrow, in light of a number of factors that I've brought to the attention of the Defence, particularly the quality of the 65 ter, an issue that's been raised time and time again. I anticipate I will be ready, I'm making every effort to do so, but this would not be an appropriate time to begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From my question you may have understood that even six or seven minutes count for the Chamber, but under the circumstances, you'll be allowed to start to cross-examine the witness tomorrow. Mr. Radojko, may I first instruct you not to speak with anyone about the evidence you have given and the evidence you are still about to give. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow, when you'll be cross-examined by counsel for the Prosecution. That would be tomorrow afternoon, quarter past 2.00, in this same courtroom. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Radojko out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would nevertheless like to use the remaining couple of minutes and see and hear from the parties, who are all well-trained common-law practitioners. Let me just put a scenario in front of you. Let's just assume that in a case the Prosecution has presented a bank transfer of 100.000 German marks with something written to it like: "For services provided." Now, the Defence calls a witness and starts examining him on how many bank accounts he has, on whether the maximum -- what would have been the maximum balance on any of his bank accounts ever, whether he would usually make his transfers through internet or whether he would write them down on paper, whether, if he would write them down on paper, whether he would put them in the mail box in branch office X or in branch office Y. But finally, Defence counsel would not tell the witness -- or ask the witness whether it ever happened to him that he made a bank transfer of 100.000 Deutschmarks with described that it was for services provided. I think there are two possibilities. Either if this would have been put to the witness, he would have said: Oh, yes, of course, I fully understand. This was a mistake by the bank. Two weeks later you find the bank transfer where the bank corrects their mistake, so that explains everything. Under those circumstances, I would not have need to know how many bank accounts the person would have had. The maximum balance at any other time would be totally irrelevant. If, of course, the core of the case would be about the transfer of 100.000 marks, I would not even want to know whether he usually makes his transfer through internet or whether he does it in writing and what branch office he needs. Now the other possibility: That witness starts rushing a bit and says: 100.000 marks, well, that's what happened often with my bank, that they make a mistake. They often write "100.000," where it's actually 10.000. But that's administration of the bank. Although it's computerised, it's a very bad administration. Then of course the next question would be: Could you give me one or two other examples where they missed one nil on their bank transfers? At least we would rapidly come to what the problem is. Either it's a mistake, either the bank is very sloppy, what would certainly need further -- should be further explored because most of the banks do not every week leave out a nil. I hope you understand what my question is. How do those experienced in the common-law tradition prevent that we have to hear evidence for a long period of time which, for one reason or another reason, may be totally irrelevant. Because if the witness later says: It was a mistake by the bank, it has been corrected two weeks afterwards, then of course the matter has been clarified sufficiently without all the other information. If, however, he says that the bank always makes this mistake with the nils or that -- he could have said: Well, my brother has a bank account. He has got the same first name, and so therefore it's explained this way, then of course we could start investigating on whether he has a brother, whether he has the same -- at least that becomes relevant, not anymore whether he transferred by wire, whether he transferred on paper, whether he used branch office A, whether he used branch office B. I am inviting the parties to assist this Chamber in seeing whether we could get the relevant information on the core issues in such a way that we do not spend much time on matters that most likely at the very end will be irrelevant. I don't know -- I said I would use the five minutes. I'm not going to ask the interpreters to stay any longer. My reputation is already bad in this respect. I would invite the parties to -- to give it one or two nights of sleep - of good sleep, I hope - and then perhaps take five minutes at lunch to see whether, even in this tradition where the truth comes to the surface quickly and -- how they would consider that -- first of all, whether you would agree with my analysis of this hypothetical case; and second, how, Mr. Josse, you would resolve the matter if you were a Prosecutor in this case or in the case of the bank account, and how you, Mr. Tieger, would resolve the matter if you were defending in the case of the transfer of 100.000 Deutschmarks. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
